items.title: Referrals and repeat sales
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: The cheapest customer to win is one you already have, or one a happy customer sends. Make repeat business easy: stay in touch, remind customers when they are due to buy again, and reward loyalty without discounting everything. Ask for referrals at the moment of delight, right after a good result, and make it easy to pass on, with a link or a card. Thank the person who referred. Track where each customer came from so you know what works. A referral works because it carries trust, so protect it: never pressure anyone, and ask only for what they are comfortable sharing.

options.text: It carries trust from someone the new customer knows
It is always free of any cost

options.text: Staying in touch and reminding customers when they are due to buy again

options.text: So you know which sources are worth more effort

items.title: Using customer feedback
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Feedback is only useful if it changes something. Gather comments from every source in one place: surveys, reviews, emails, calls and what staff hear. Look for themes, because one comment is a story and ten the same is a pattern. Separate quick fixes from bigger changes and decide which to do first by how many customers it affects and how much it matters to them. Give each chosen change an owner and a date, and tell customers what you changed because of what they said. Keep the record, so you can see over time whether the same complaint returns.

items.title: Collecting feedback
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: To learn what customers think, ask them and make it easy. Ask soon after the experience, while it is fresh, with a few short questions: one score, and one open question such as "What one thing would improve this?". Use more than one route: a quick message after a sale, a card, a call to a few customers, and review sites. Ask unhappy customers as well as happy ones, because they show what to fix. Do not argue with answers; thank people and note them. A low response is common, so keep asking and keep it short.

options.text: Soon after their experience, while it is fresh

options.text: What one thing would improve this?

options.text: Thank them and note it, without arguing

items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Reviews and case studies let new customers see evidence from people like them. Ask for a review soon after a good result, make it easy with a direct link, and never offer payment in return for a positive one or write fake reviews, which are unfair and can be illegal. Reply to every review politely, including bad ones: it shows how you treat people. A case study tells one customer's story: the problem, what you did and the result, ideally with numbers and a quote, and always with permission. Show them where buyers decide, such as your website and listings.

items.body: A tender is a formal invitation to offer to supply goods or services, often to public bodies and larger firms. First decide whether to bid: do you meet every must-have, can you deliver on time and can you profit at the likely price? Read the documents completely and note the deadline, because late bids are usually rejected. Answer every question directly, in the order and format asked, with evidence such as examples and figures. Show how you would deliver, and what could go wrong. Price to cover your costs and a fair margin. Check, ideally by someone who did not write it, and submit early.

items.title: Accessibility for customers
items.source: Draft for review. Written by an AI assistant from general UK small-business knowledge, not from a cited document. Check every fact against current GOV.UK and regulator guidance, and have someone who does this work review it, before it is activated. Rules differ by country and change.
items.body: Accessibility means making your premises, website and service usable by everyone, including disabled people. In the UK, businesses that provide services must not discriminate and must make reasonable adjustments, which can be as simple as a ramp, clear signs, large print, quiet times or help on request. For websites, use clear headings, good contrast, text descriptions for images, captions for video, and make everything usable with a keyboard. Ask disabled customers what would help and test with real users. Train staff to offer help without assuming. Good accessibility helps many others too, such as older people and parents with prams.
